Zealous
zĕl´us
adj. (fervent, ardent; rendering Greek zelotes)
From Greek zelos, heat, fervour. Zeal is a temperature, and Scripture is careful to ask what the heat is for.

Biblical Definition

Zealous means burning with earnestness. Scripture treats it as a raw force needing direction: Paul testifies that his countrymen “have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2), and he had himself persecuted the church out of exactly that zeal. Rightly aimed, it is required — Christ redeems for Himself “a peculiar people, zealous of good works” (Tit 2:14) — and its absence draws the harshest verdict in the letters to the churches: “because thou art lukewarm… be zealous therefore, and repent” (Rev 3:16,19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines zealous as warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object; and warmly engaged in religion.

expand to see more

ZEALOUS, a. Warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object.

2. Warm; ardent; fervent; as zealous love; zealous devotion.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:2 — "For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge."

Tit 2:14 — "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works."

Rev 3:19 — "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent."

Gal 4:18 — "But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you."

Modern Corruption

Two failures sit side by side: zeal without knowledge, which does damage in God's name, and knowledge without zeal, which Christ threatens to spew out of His mouth.

expand to see more

Romans 10:2 is Paul's charitable and devastating assessment of his own nation: they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. He is not calling them insincere; he is saying sincerity is not the question. Zeal is a fire, and a fire in the hearth warms the house while the same fire in the roof destroys it. Every persecution the church has suffered from religious people, and every harm the church has done to others, has run on genuine zeal aimed wrongly.

But the opposite error is the one Christ addresses to a church rather than to unbelievers, and He uses stronger language for it. Laodicea was neither cold nor hot, and the remedy prescribed is not more information but temperature: be zealous therefore, and repent. A congregation that has traded fervour for respectability has not become mature; it has become the one thing in Revelation that provokes nausea.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zelotes (G2207), a zealot, one burning with zeal; zeloo (G2206), to be fervent — capable of holy jealousy or of envy, depending on its object.

expand to see more

Greek zelotes (G2207) — zealous one; Acts 22:3, Titus 2:14, 1 Corinthians 14:12.

Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, fervour; John 2:17, the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.

Greek zeloo (G2206) — to be zealous; Revelation 3:19, and Galatians 4:18, it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing.

Usage

"“A zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” — sincerity is not the question."

"“A peculiar people, zealous of good works” — zeal with an assigned direction."

"“Be zealous therefore, and repent” — the cure for lukewarm."
